notes.meaning: Paul answers a question from the Corinthians about the relief fund for poor believers in Jerusalem. He instructs them to follow the same plan he gave to the churches in Galatia. By calling the Jerusalem Christians 'saints' (God's holy people), he reminds them that they are helping their own brothers and sisters in faith.

Paul directs each person to put aside some money at home on the first day of every week, giving in proportion to their earnings. Saving regularly meant no frantic, last-minute collections would be needed when he arrived. The believers gathered on Sunday because that was the day the Lord Jesus rose from the dead.

The Corinthian church was to choose trusted representatives to carry the collection to Jerusalem. Paul promised to write letters of recommendation to introduce these messengers to the leaders there. Involving church-chosen messengers ensured complete honesty and kept anyone from suspecting that money was mishandled.

Paul adds that if the collection turns out to be large enough to justify his presence, he will travel along with the church's messengers. He was careful not to take charge of the money alone, keeping himself completely above suspicion. This encouraged the Corinthians to give generously while guarding trust and integrity.

Paul shares his travel plans, explaining that he will visit Corinth after passing through Macedonia. He had changed an earlier route so he could encourage the Macedonian churches on his way. He wanted the Corinthians to know his visit was genuine and carefully planned.

Paul hoped to stay with the Corinthians for a good while, possibly even spending the entire winter with them. When the time came for him to move on, the church could help provide what he needed for his next journey. He wanted a warm, unhurried visit that would allow them to care for one another.

Paul explains that he does not want a brief, passing visit right now. He hopes to stay long enough for a meaningful visit, but only if the Lord allows it. He reminds believers to submit all their personal plans humbly to God's will.

Paul decides to stay in the city of Ephesus until the late spring festival of Pentecost. This note shows that he wrote this letter from Ephesus rather than from Macedonia. He used well-known Jewish calendar dates to describe the seasons of his travels.

God had opened a wide doorway in Ephesus for Paul to preach the gospel with great results. Even though many enemies opposed him there, he saw that opposition as a reason to stay rather than run away. Big opportunities to serve God often bring real spiritual resistance.

Paul asks the church to welcome Timothy warmly and give him no reason to be afraid. Timothy was young and might easily feel intimidated by a church known for its arguments and pride. Since Timothy was doing the Lord's work just like Paul, he deserved safety and kindness.

Paul warns the believers not to treat Timothy with contempt because of his youth. When his visit ended, they were to send him off peacefully and help supply his travel needs so he could return to Paul. Faithful ministers of the gospel deserve respect and honor from the people they serve.

Paul had strongly urged Apollos to visit Corinth with the other brothers, but Apollos chose not to go at that time. Apollos knew that some Corinthians were using his name to form a divisive faction, so he wisely stayed away to avoid making the division worse. Paul respected his co-worker's freedom and showed no personal jealousy toward him.

Paul gives four rapid commands that sound like an officer calling soldiers to attention. Believers must stay alert against spiritual dangers, remain firm in gospel truth, show courage under pressure, and be strong in the Lord. Christians must not drop their guard when temptations and false teachings surround them.

Paul immediately balances courage and strength by commanding that every single action be done in love. Boldness without love can easily turn into harsh fighting and selfish pride. Love must be the guiding motive behind everything a Christian does.

Stephanas and his family were among the very first converts in their region, and they devoted their lives to serving fellow believers. Paul urges the church to respect and follow leaders like them, along with anyone else who works hard for the gospel. True Christian leadership is earned through humble, selfless service.

Paul rejoices because Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus had arrived to visit him in Ephesus. Their arrival made up for the sadness of being separated from the Corinthian church. These three men had likely carried the letter of questions that Paul answers in this epistle.

These three visitors refreshed Paul's spirit, which in turn brought comfort to the Corinthian church. Paul tells the believers to give proper recognition and honor to people who serve like this. Christians should be quick to appreciate those who bring peace and encouragement to God's people.

Churches throughout the Roman province around Ephesus sent their warm greetings to Corinth. Aquila and Prisca, who had once lived in Corinth, sent special Christian love along with the congregation that gathered in their home. Early Christians regularly met in private houses for worship before dedicated church buildings existed.

All the believers in Ephesus sent their greetings, and Paul urged the Corinthians to greet one another with a holy kiss. This was a normal cultural sign of peace and family affection that symbolized true unity among believers. It called the Corinthians to lay aside their quarrels and show genuine love to one another.

Paul took the pen and wrote this greeting with his own hand. He usually dictated his letters to a secretary, but signing with his own handwriting proved the letter was genuinely from him. This protected the church from forged letters and added a warm, personal touch.

Paul gives a solemn warning that anyone who does not love the Lord is under God's judgment and cut off. He then adds the early Christian prayer 'Maranatha,' which means 'Our Lord, come!' Sincere love for Jesus is the true test of faith, and believers look forward to the day of His return.

Paul pronounces a final blessing, praying that the grace—the unearned favor and kindness—of the Lord Jesus will rest on them. Even after correcting many serious faults throughout the letter, he wraps the church in Christ's forgiving grace. God's grace is the daily strength that every believer needs.

Paul ends the letter by sending his personal love to everyone in the church through Christ Jesus. His hard corrections had not come from anger, but from a sincere love for their spiritual health. He wanted them to know that, despite all their struggles, they remained deeply loved.
